title: Text & Output
description: Print text, inspect the system, and start composing commands.

levels.title: Printing text — echo
levels.lesson:
`echo` prints its arguments back to the screen. It's the simplest way to produce output in bash:

```
echo Hello, world!
echo "Paths with spaces need quotes"
```

You'll use it constantly in scripts to display messages, debug values, and write content into files (that comes later).

levels.title: Who am I? — whoami
levels.lesson:
`whoami` prints the name of the **current user** — the account you're logged in as.

On a shared server this matters a lot: it tells you whose permissions you have, and whether you need `sudo` (run as administrator) for a given task.

On this system, you're always `user`.

levels.title: Reading multiple files — cat
levels.lesson:
You've already used `cat` on one file. Pass it several and it prints them **back to back**, in order:

```
cat /etc/hostname /etc/hosts
```

This is where `cat` earns its "concatenate" name — it chains files together in one stream of output.

challenge.instruction: Print both `/etc/hostname` and `/etc/hosts` in a single `cat` command.

levels.title: Combining commands — pipes (preview)
levels.lesson:
Pipes (`|`) let you feed the output of one command directly into another. This is one of the most powerful ideas in the shell — instead of one command that does everything, you chain small commands that each do one thing well.

```
ls | sort
echo "hello" | cat
```

Full pipe support is coming in the next unit. This level is a preview — read the lesson and move on.
